metadata.dsm5_code: F32.89 (other specified depressive disorder due to substance/medication)
metadata.icd10_code: F1x.94 (psychoactive substance-induced mood disorder, depressive type)

aeo.what_is: Depression caused by drugs, alcohol, withdrawal or medicines. It usually improves once the substance is stopped.

content.temporal_criteria: Depressive symptoms must develop during or soon after substance intoxication, withdrawal, or medication exposure. Symptoms typically improve within days to weeks (approximately one month) after full cessation of the substance. If symptoms persist substantially longer after stopping, consider a primary depressive disorder.

confused_with: Major Depressive Disorder (primary) — the key is timing and causality. If depression episodes occurred before substance use began, persist long after cessation (more than a month), or happen during sustained abstinence, it's likely primary MDD. Substance-induced depression is tied to exposure and resolves with abstinence.

Adjustment Disorder — adjustment disorder involves emotional response to life stress. Substance-induced depression has a direct pharmacological cause (the substance itself), not just the stress of dealing with substance use.
Bipolar Depression — if someone has a history of hypomania or mania, depressive symptoms during withdrawal (especially stimulants) may be part of a bipolar disorder. Careful history is essential.

Delirium — delirium involves fluctuating consciousness, confusion, and disorientation during severe intoxication or withdrawal. Substance-induced depression involves persistent low mood with clear consciousness.

Normal withdrawal dysphoria — brief sadness, fatigue, or irritability during early withdrawal is common and expected. Substance-induced depressive disorder meets full criteria for a depressive syndrome with significant impairment.
misdiagnosis_explained.clarifying_factors: Detailed substance timeline (what, when, how much, when stopped); history of depressive episodes before substance use; collateral from family about baseline mood; urine toxicology; medication review (beta-blockers, corticosteroids, interferons, isotretinoin); symptoms improving with abstinence; distinguishing transient withdrawal from full depressive syndrome.
misdiagnosis_explained.timeline_differences: Major depression (MDD) can happen at any time and isn't tied to a substance. Substance-induced depression follows using a substance, a higher dose, or withdrawal, and gets better after stopping. Adjustment disorder is linked to a stressful event and lasts a limited time. The low, uneasy mood of withdrawal goes away within days; substance-induced depression can last weeks.
misdiagnosis_explained.impairment_differences: Both cause real problems in daily life. The difference is the cause and how it is expected to go. Substance-induced depression should clear up after stopping the substance, with support, while major depression needs ongoing mental health treatment even without substances.

description.overview: Depression in which low mood, losing interest or pleasure, and related changes in sleep, appetite, energy and thinking start while using a substance, during withdrawal, or soon after, or after taking a medicine known to cause these effects. The depression is linked in time to the substance or medicine, causes real distress or problems in daily life, and is not better explained by depression that would happen on its own.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A 28-year-old stops using cocaine after years of daily use. Within days, he feels profoundly depressed, exhausted, anhedonic, and hopeless. He sleeps 12 hours a day and has suicidal thoughts. After three weeks of abstinence, therapy, and support, his mood gradually improves.

A 50-year-old woman starts interferon therapy for hepatitis C. Three weeks in, she develops severe depression, fatigue, and hopelessness. Her infectious disease doctor consults psychiatry, who starts an antidepressant. She completes the life-saving treatment with mood support, and depression resolves when interferon ends.

A 35-year-old with alcohol use disorder goes into detox. During withdrawal, he has a very low, uneasy mood, anxiety, and thoughts of suicide. After medically supervised detox, naltrexone, and CBT to prevent relapse, his mood settles without long-term antidepressants.

A 22-year-old quits heavy daily cannabis use and within a week feels depressed, irritable, has no appetite, and can't sleep. She thinks she's 'broken.' Her therapist explains it's withdrawal-related depression. With sleep hygiene, exercise, and supportive therapy, she feels normal again within a month.

A 40-year-old man is prescribed a beta-blocker for high blood pressure. Within weeks, he feels low, fatigued, and loses interest in hobbies. His doctor switches him to a different blood pressure medication, and his mood improves within days.

A 25-year-old taking isotretinoin for acne develops low mood, loses interest in things she enjoyed, and has crying spells. Her dermatologist recognizes medicine-induced depression, stops the isotretinoin, and refers her to a psychiatrist. Her mood returns to normal within two weeks.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that the depression is caused by a substance and may resolve with abstinence.
Fear that they've permanently damaged their brain with substance use.
Frustration if the substance is medically necessary and there are no alternatives.
Confusion about whether it's 'real' depression or just withdrawal.
Hope that staying sober will prevent future episodes.
Guilt or shame about substance use causing the depression.
Worry about whether underlying depression will emerge once the substance is cleared.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Prominent and persistent depressed mood and/or markedly diminished interest or pleasure with associated depressive symptoms. B. Evidence from history, physical exam, or labs that (1) symptoms developed during or soon after intoxication, withdrawal, or medication use; and (2) the substance/medication is capable of producing the symptoms. C. Not better explained by an independent depressive disorder (e.g., symptoms preceded use, persist for a substantial period—about one month—after cessation, or there is other evidence for a non-substance cause). D. Does not occur exclusively during delirium. E. Causes clinically significant distress or impairment.
content.prevalence: How common it is depends on the substance, how much and how long it is used, and the person. It is common with alcohol, sedatives and opioids, and during withdrawal from stimulants or benzodiazepines. It has also been reported with several prescription medicines.
content.age_of_onset: It can start at any age, depending on when the substance or medicine is used. It often appears between the late teens and middle adulthood, when substance use and medicine use are more common.
content.prognosis: Typically improves within days to weeks after cessation and stabilization. Risk of recurrence with re-exposure is high. In vulnerable individuals, an episode may unmask or trigger a primary mood disorder requiring ongoing treatment.

circuitry: Acute and subacute dysregulation of fronto-limbic networks (prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, amygdala, hippocampus) during intoxication/withdrawal.
The brain's reward system (ventral striatum) becomes less active after long-term use, which adds to losing interest or pleasure in things.
neurochemistry: Monoaminergic depletion or receptor downregulation (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine) after chronic exposure or withdrawal.

Rebound changes in calming and activating brain chemicals (GABA and glutamate), for example with alcohol or benzodiazepines, and an overactive stress-hormone system (HPA axis), which cause a low, uneasy mood and anxiety.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Family mood disorder risk, early adversity, sleep/circadian disruption, and high-stress environments increase susceptibility to substance-related mood effects.

history_psychosocial: Detailed timeline aligning depressive symptoms with intoxication, withdrawal, dose changes, or new medications.
Comprehensive substance history (type, amount, route, frequency, last use) and prior responses.
Past psychiatric history (episodes without substance exposure), family history, safety assessment (suicidality), and functional impact.
medical_assessment: Focused physical and neurological exam; review prescribed/OTC/herbal agents.
Targeted labs: CBC, CMP, TSH; urine toxicology; pregnancy test when relevant; medication levels as indicated.
Consider sleep apnea screening, hepatic/renal function for medication planning.
standardized_measures: C-SSRS for suicide risk; AUDIT/DAST for substance screening.
risk_stratification: Hospitalize/urgent care for suicidal intent/plan, psychosis, catatonia, severe withdrawal, or inability to care for self.
Assess overdose risk, intoxication, and withdrawal complications.
differential_diagnosis: Primary Major Depressive Disorder (episodes independent of exposure).
Depressive disorder due to another medical condition.
Delirium or memory and thinking decline (neurocognitive disorder); being intoxicated or in withdrawal without full depression.
evaluation.team_and_process: Coordinate psychiatry with addiction medicine, primary care, and prescribing specialists. Establish a unified plan for cessation/taper, withdrawal management, and mood monitoring.

core: Low mood and/or losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy
Feeling restless, or moving and thinking slowly
Feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt
contextual_features: Temporal linkage to intoxication, dose escalation, or withdrawal
Cravings, a low or uneasy mood, and low energy in the early days after stopping

severity_levels.mild: Symptoms beyond a usual hangover or low, uneasy mood, with limited effect on daily life; can usually be managed with outpatient care.
severity_levels.moderate: Clear impairment; may require medication plus psychotherapy and close follow-up.
severity_levels.severe: Marked impairment, suicidality, psychotic features, or medically significant withdrawal; consider higher level of care.

biological: High-dose or chronic exposure to depressogenic substances or medications
psychological: Impulsivity, trauma history, poor coping skills
environmental: Ready access to substances; unstable housing or employment

impact_on_life.school_work: Absenteeism, presenteeism, errors, and disciplinary issues related to use/withdrawal and mood.
impact_on_life.medical: Poor adherence to care; overdose/withdrawal complications; interaction risks.
impact_on_life.emotional: Shame, guilt, demoralization, and relapse risk.

comorbidities: Substance Use Disorders (alcohol, opioids, sedatives, stimulants, cannabis)

address_exposure: Stop or taper the offending substance/medication when safe and feasible.
Medically supervised detoxification/withdrawal management if indicated.
Substitute with non-depressogenic alternatives after risk–benefit review.
psychotherapy: Motivational Interviewing (MI) and relapse prevention (CBT for SUD).
Behavioral activation, to help with losing interest or pleasure and with inactivity.
CBT or IPT for mood; integrate contingency management where available.
medications: Antidepressants may help when symptoms are severe, last beyond the early weeks after stopping, or depression seems separate from the substance. SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine) are usually tried first; SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) when pain or tiredness stand out; bupropion for low energy (not used with a risk of seizures or eating disorders, or during heavy alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal); mirtazapine for poor sleep or low appetite.
Avoid initiating antidepressants during acute severe intoxication/withdrawal unless clinically necessary; reassess after stabilization.
For alcohol or opioid use disorders, consider FDA-approved SUD pharmacotherapies (e.g., naltrexone, acamprosate; buprenorphine or methadone) alongside mood treatment.
Care is taken with drug interactions, heart-rhythm changes that can be dangerous (seen on an ECG), and effects on weight and blood sugar; doses may be adjusted for liver or kidney problems.
neuromodulation: ECT for severe depression, depression with losing touch with reality, catatonia, or suicidal depression, when a fast response is needed or medicines should not be used.
rTMS as an add-on when depression hasn't improved with other treatment, once substance use is stable.
lifestyle_interventions: Sleep/circadian regularization; structured daily activity and exercise.
Nutrition/hydration restoration; thiamine in alcohol use risk.
Peer recovery supports (12-step/SMART), craving management, and trigger planning.
care_coordination: Collaborate with addiction services, prescribing clinicians, and primary care.
Safety planning for suicidality; means restriction; frequent early follow-up.

treatment_goals: Achieve abstinence or safe discontinuation/taper of the offending agent.
Relieve depressive symptoms and restore functioning.
Prevent relapse of substance use and depressive episodes.
Establish sustainable recovery supports and monitoring.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Failure to obtain a precise timeline linking symptoms to exposure/withdrawal.
Attributing all symptoms to a primary mood disorder without considering substances or medications.
Overlooking iatrogenic contributors (e.g., interferon-alpha, isotretinoin, corticosteroids, varenicline).
overdiagnosis_factors: Labeling primary MDD as substance-induced when depressive episodes predate exposure or persist well beyond cessation.
Mistaking a brief low, uneasy mood during withdrawal for full depression.
Diagnosing during delirium or acute intoxication without reassessment after stabilization.
warning_signs: Suicidal ideation/behavior during intoxication or early abstinence.
Severe trouble sleeping, agitation, or moving and thinking very slowly during withdrawal.
Rapid relapse to substance use to self-medicate mood symptoms.
self_help_strategies: Track mood relative to use/medication timing to identify triggers.
Use recovery supports and coping plans for high-risk times (e.g., evenings, paydays).
Prioritize sleep, nutrition, hydration, and daily activity; schedule pleasant events.
Build a crisis/safety plan and share with supports.

adolescence: Depression may follow binge episodes or cannabis/stimulant use; strong family/school involvement improves outcomes.
adulthood: Common with alcohol or prescription medications; workplace and relationship impairment prominent.
older_adults: Higher risk of medication-induced depression (polypharmacy); careful review of agents like beta-blockers, corticosteroids, interferons.

first_person_statements: When I stopped using, I felt worse than I ever had. I didn't know if it was withdrawal or if I was just broken. Thankfully, it got better with time.
The interferon made me so depressed I wanted to die, but stopping wasn't an option. Adding an antidepressant saved me.
I thought the alcohol was helping my depression, but it was actually causing it. Once I got sober, I felt better than I had in years.
Quitting weed made me feel terrible for weeks. I almost went back to using because I couldn't stand feeling so low, but my therapist helped me push through.
I had no idea a blood pressure medication could cause depression. Switching to a different one was like flipping a switch—I felt like myself again.
The hardest part was not knowing if the depression would go away. Once I understood it was the substance, I could have hope that it was temporary.

comparisons: It's like your brain is trying to recalibrate after being chemically altered—everything feels off and dark until the system resets.
Imagine your mood as a plant that's been poisoned: it looks dead and withered, but once you remove the toxin and give it time, it can recover.
Think of it as your brain running on low battery because the substance drained it—once you stop the substance and 'recharge,' you start to feel normal again.
It's like a fog that rolls in when you start (or stop) a substance, making everything seem gray and hopeless, and then lifts when the substance clears.

faqs.question: How do I know if my depression is substance-induced or primary?
faqs.answer: The key is timing. If depression started during or after substance use (or withdrawal) and improves within weeks of abstinence, it's likely substance-induced. If you had depression before substance use or it persists long after stopping (more than a month), it may be primary MDD.

faqs.question: What substances commonly cause depression?
faqs.answer: Alcohol, opioids, sedatives (benzodiazepines, sleep aids), cannabis, and stimulants (especially during withdrawal). Medications like corticosteroids, beta-blockers, interferons, isotretinoin, and some hormonal contraceptives can also cause depression.

faqs.question: How long does it take for depression to improve after stopping a substance?
faqs.answer: It varies. Most improve within days to weeks. Stimulant withdrawal depression may resolve in 1–2 weeks. Alcohol or opioid withdrawal can take several weeks. Medication-induced depression often improves within days to weeks after stopping the drug.

faqs.question: Do I need antidepressants if my depression is substance-induced?
faqs.answer: Not always. If symptoms are severe or persistent, antidepressants may help. For milder cases, supportive therapy, abstinence, sleep, nutrition, and time may be enough. If a medication must be continued (like interferon), antidepressants are often added.

faqs.question: Can I use that substance or medication again?
faqs.answer: Recreational substances should generally be avoided. If it's a necessary medication, your doctor may try alternatives or use the lowest effective dose with psychiatric support. Re-exposure carries high risk of recurrence.

faqs.question: What if I can't stop the substance (like a needed medication)?
faqs.answer: Your medical team can explore alternatives, reduce doses, or add an antidepressant to manage mood while continuing necessary treatment. Close collaboration between prescribers and psychiatry is key.

faqs.question: Is substance-induced depression serious?
faqs.answer: Yes. It can be just as severe as primary depression, including suicidal ideation and functional impairment. It requires serious treatment and monitoring, even if it's expected to resolve.

faqs.question: Can withdrawal alone cause depression without ongoing use?
faqs.answer: Yes. Withdrawal from alcohol, opioids, sedatives, stimulants, and cannabis can all cause depressive symptoms. This is a form of substance-induced depression. It typically improves within weeks as the brain readjusts.

faqs.question: What if I feel suicidal during withdrawal?
faqs.answer: This is a medical emergency. Contact your doctor, go to an ER, or call 988. Withdrawal depression can include severe suicidal ideation, and immediate support and monitoring are essential.

faqs.question: Can alcohol cause depression even while drinking?
faqs.answer: Yes. Chronic alcohol use can cause depression during active use (not just withdrawal). Alcohol is a depressant that disrupts neurotransmitters and worsens mood over time.

faqs.question: How can I tell if I have both substance-induced and primary depression?
faqs.answer: This is common. If you had depression before substance use, during abstinence, or symptoms persist well beyond expected recovery time, you may have both. Comprehensive evaluation and treatment of both conditions is needed.

faqs.question: Will my brain go back to normal after stopping?
faqs.answer: For most people, yes. The brain has significant capacity to heal with sustained abstinence. However, prolonged heavy use of some substances can cause lasting changes. Early intervention and abstinence improve outcomes.

faqs.question: Should I wait out the depression or get help immediately?
faqs.answer: Get help. Even if it's expected to resolve, monitoring for safety (especially suicidal ideation) and supportive treatment (therapy, medication if needed, structure, social support) improve recovery and prevent relapse.

faqs.question: Can over-the-counter medications or supplements cause depression?
faqs.answer: Yes. High doses of antihistamines, certain pain relievers (overuse), and interactions between supplements and medications can contribute to mood changes. Always review all substances with your doctor.

faqs.question: What can I do to help myself during recovery?
faqs.answer: Prioritize sleep, nutrition, and hydration. Engage in light physical activity (walking, yoga). Attend therapy or recovery support groups (AA, SMART, etc.). Avoid isolation. Be patient—mood improvement takes time. Build a safety plan and share it with supports.

real_life_examples.person: A 27-year-old man stopped heavy daily cannabis use after five years. Within a week, he had low mood, lost interest in things, couldn't sleep, and lost his appetite. He felt hopeless and thought he'd never feel normal. His therapist explained withdrawal-related depression and started CBT and a regular sleep routine. With exercise and support, his mood improved within three weeks, and he's stayed off cannabis for a year.

A 52-year-old woman started interferon-alpha therapy for hepatitis C. Three weeks in, she reported profound fatigue, hopelessness, and thoughts of ending her life. Her hepatologist consulted psychiatry, who started escitalopram and provided weekly supportive therapy. She completed the life-saving antiviral treatment with mood support, and her depression fully resolved when interferon ended.

A 35-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder came in with a very low, uneasy mood, anxiety, and thoughts of suicide during withdrawal. He went through medically supervised detox, then started naltrexone for alcohol use disorder and CBT to prevent relapse. His mood improved a lot within two weeks of not drinking, and he's been sober and free of depression for eight months.

A 22-year-old woman quit heavy cannabis use and within days felt depressed, irritable, couldn't sleep, and had no appetite. She feared she'd damaged her brain permanently. Her therapist explained it was cannabis withdrawal and started supportive therapy with sleep hygiene and activity scheduling. Within a month, she felt 'like herself again' and continues therapy to prevent relapse.

A 40-year-old man started a beta-blocker for hypertension. Within weeks, he felt fatigued, low, and lost interest in his hobbies. His primary care doctor recognized medication-induced depression and switched him to an ACE inhibitor. His mood improved within days, and he's been stable on the new medication for two years.

content.when_to_seek_help: Get checked soon if serious depression starts with a new medicine, a dose change, while using a substance, or during withdrawal. Get urgent help for thoughts of suicide or plans to act on them, losing touch with reality, catatonia (being unable to move or respond normally), or severe withdrawal symptoms.

positive_factors: Early identification and removal/taper of the offending agent
Engagement in SUD treatment and recovery supports
Strong social network and stable housing
challenging_factors: Co-occurring primary mood or anxiety disorders
Other medical conditions, long-term pain, and sleep disorders
